title: Slot reuse simulations — cudaMallocAsync pressure and OOM sensitivity notes
content:
Purpose:
This doc captures a set of focused simulations and field experiments around slot reuse and allocator pressure when using cudaMallocAsync (CMA). Goal: understand transient OOMs and fragmentation growth patterns seen in production pools when workload mixes small transient allocations (attention scratch, temporary activations) with long-lived KV cache entries.

High-level hypothesis summary:
- CMA pools create arena slots that are long-lived and can become unusable for new allocations if the slot layout fragments across different size classes (slot fragmentation).
- Long-lived KV cache allocations pinned into large arena slots block coalescing, causing tail chunking and repeated cudaMallocAsync fallback to raw cudaMalloc (which is expensive and spikes latency or fails under pressure).
- Eviction heuristics that trigger only on memory pressure are too reactive; proactive slot compaction (or reserved tail pools) reduces OOM spikes.

Environment / baseline:
- HW: NVIDIA A100-SXM4 80GB (hosting pool nodes), 8 GPUs per node in Dedicated capacity env.
- Driver: NVIDIA 545.x; CUDA toolkit 12.2; cuMallocAsync enabled in runtime build.
- Serving runtime: rwinf-serving v2.7.1 (dev branch used for experiments: pr/1892), allocator build flags: -DUSE_CUDAMALLOCASYNC=1 -DENABLE_ARENA_SAMPLING=1.
- Model: Llama-2-13B quantized (4-bit), default kv-cache enabled. Sequence profiles: 90% short (<128 tokens), 10% long (512–2048 tokens) with 1:10 ratio of batch short-to-long.
- Typical request mix used: bursty-batch pattern (arrivals with bursts of 12 concurrent requests every 2–3s).

Experiment matrix (major runs):
- Run A: default CMA pools (arena_size=256MB, max_arenas=8), eviction disabled except on OOM.
- Run B: CMA with aggressive eviction (idle_age_ms=500, test only), same arena_size.
- Run C: CMA with mixed slab sizing (small-slab=32KB, med=1MB, large=64MB) and pre-reserve tail slab of 1GB per-gpu.
- Run D: Fallback to caching allocator (cudaMalloc/cudaFree caching) - baseline comparison.
Each run: 6-hour soak, captured telemetry at 1s resolution (alloc/free events, arena histograms, resident pages, OOM events, retry counts).

What we measured (telemetry sources):
- allocator.alloc_size distribution and sequence of alloc/free per stream (sampled).
- arena.free-gap histogram (per-arena fragmentation map).
- cudaMallocAsync fallback events (where runtime had to call raw cudaMalloc).
- eviction_count and eviction_size/time.
- per-request tail latency P50/P95/P99 and per-token cpu/gpu time.
- OOMs: Type (retryable vs non-retryable), stack/trace sample of allocation site.
Telemetry queries used: (examples)
- BigQuery: SELECT bin, COUNT(*) FROM allocator_events WHERE event='free' GROUP BY bin ORDER BY bin;
- Prom query: sum(rate(runtime_cma_fallback_total[1m])) by (pool)

Key observations and notes:
1) Tail-chunking pattern (new):
  - Observed frequent small allocations at inference step boundaries (~8–48KB) that are short-lived (<10ms). These are typically scratch buffers for fused-kernels and attention scratch.
  - When these short allocations occur near long-lived KV cache allocations (size class ~4–16MB), the allocator places them in the same arena but in gaps that cannot be merged later because the preceding/following slots are pinned. Over time (minutes to hours), the number of unusable tiny gaps increases → tail chunking.
  - CMA does not compact by default; reclamation only returns whole arenas to CUDA when entire arena is unused. This matches our observed growth of resident memory without usable capacity.

2) CMA fallback cascade:
  - Under fragmentation, allocator attempts to fulfill small allocation by finding slots; when none found in current arenas it asks CMA to grow arena or request raw cudaMalloc. Raw cudaMalloc takes ~4–10 ms on A100 in our env and sometimes returns CUDA_ERROR_OUT_OF_MEMORY under sustained pressure.
  - Observed correlated spikes: increase in raw cudaMalloc calls precedes a burst of retryable OOMs. The runtime then stalls requests, triggers evictions, and sometimes falls into a retry loop that spikes latency.

3) Eviction timing sensitivity:
  - Aggressive eviction (Run B) reduces resident fragmentation by ~30% vs Run A, but increases tail latency P99 by ~12% during eviction windows because eviction work steals GPU cycles and kernels see L2 changes.
  - Eviction that is synchronous on allocation path is catastrophic for latency; asynchronous background eviction with rate limits is acceptable.

4) Slot reuse heuristics that helped: 
  - Per-stream slab affinity: keeping short-lived scratch allocations constrained to a small per-stream slab (32KB–1MB) reduced fragmentation growth by ~40%.
  - Warm tail-reserve: reserving a 1GB reserved tail pool per GPU that only scratch allocations use prevented CMA from co-locating KV cache entries into those arenas. This increased steady-state resident by +1GB but reduced OOM incidence and cudaMalloc fallbacks by ~85%. Cost trade-off is predictable.
  - Allocation sampling to detect hot slots: we applied a lightweight profiler that marks slots as "hot" if their occupant lived >T_hot_ms. Hot slots are treated as immovable; the runtime avoids packing short allocations near hot slots by preferring dedicated small slabs. This reduced fragmentation entropy in arena histograms.

Quantitative numbers (representative):
- Run A (default CMA): average resident 62.1GB; fragmentation metric (unusable_gap_bytes / resident) = 11.2%; raw cudaMalloc fallback rate = 0.9/min; OOM events = 13 in 6h (7 non-retryable).
- Run B (aggressive eviction): resident 58.6GB; fragmentation = 7.6%; fallback = 0.15/min; OOMs = 4 (1 non-retryable); P99 latency delta +12% during evict windows.
- Run C (tail-reserve + per-stream slabs): resident 63.4GB (+1.3GB reserved); fragmentation = 3.1%; fallback = 0.03/min; OOMs = 0 in 6h; P99 latency stable.
- Run D (caching allocator (raw caching)): resident 66.2GB; fragmentation metric not applicable; fallback 0; OOMs = 2 (non-retryable), average allocation latency higher.

Actionable mitigations (short-term):
- Introduce a per-GPU reserved tail slab (configurable, default 1GB) for ephemeral scratch allocations. This is a safe default for hosted pools where predictable OOM avoidance matters.
- Implement per-stream small-slab allocator for transient allocations (32KB–2MB), with a fast-path that never touches large arenas.
- Make CMA fallback metrics (raw-cudaMalloc counts and retryable OOMs) part of SLO/alerting (alert on >0.5 rawMalloc/min sustained for 5m).
- Add sampling-based slot heatmap in telemetry to visualize fraction of slots older than T_hot (configurable).

Actionable mitigations (medium-term):
- Arena compaction experiment: implement background compaction that tries to migrate movable allocations out of fragmented arenas during low utilization windows. Migration must be cooperative (support for CUDA memcpy between device memory ranges + update pointers in runtime). Complex but addresses root cause.
- Smart slab sizing: auto-tune slab size distribution based on observed allocation size histogram (adaptive slab tiers).

Open questions / unknowns to validate:
- Migration safety around pinned tensors and third-party kernels that hold raw device pointers: if we move memory we must either provide indirection or update kernel code to accept relocatable handles. Costly.
- Does CMA behavior differ across driver versions in ways that matter? We observed slight differences between 545.x and 520.x (older) but need systematic matrix across drivers and CUDA versions.
- Interaction with Multi-Process Service (MPS) and CUDA streams: does per-stream slab affinity conflict with multi-tenancy across processes? We need a cross-process coordination story for Dedicated pools with container per-customer.

Experiment artifacts and reproducibility notes (how to reproduce quickly):
1) Repro script (simplified):
  - workload generator (python) that replays allocation/free traces captured from production (trace id: trace-20250608-34). Command: python tools/replay_alloc_trace.py --trace traces/trace-20250608-34.json --gpu 0 --rate-burst 12 --seed 42
  - runtime build with CMA enabled: bazel build //runtime:serving --config=cudamallocasync && sudo systemctl restart rwinf-serving
  - telemetry capture: ./tools/capture_allocator_events.sh --duration 6h --out runs/run-A.json
2) Key logs to collect: allocator_events.log, nvprof/ncu traces around fallback events, dmesg (OOM logs), runtime-perf counters.

Quick checklist for eng owners (what to do next):
- [ ] Roll out per-GPU tail-reserve as feature flag to canary pool for 48h. (Owner: Maya)
- [ ] Add raw-cudaMalloc fallback alert to infra SRE playbook. (Owner: Jonah)
- [ ] Prototype per-stream small slab allocator (PoC in pr/1892). Measure P95/P99 overhead. (Owner: Ethan)
- [ ] Schedule driver/CUDA matrix runs (545.x, 530.x, 520.x × CUDA 12.x/11.x). (Owner: Priya)
- [ ] Draft design doc for background arena compaction (investigate pointer indirection cost). (Owner: Priya + research)

Notes from experiments worth preserving (rough bullet log):
- 2025-06-11 10:23: observed first retryable OOM on run A at throughput 220 qps; raw mallocs rose from 0.1/min to 3/min over 2m window.
- 2025-06-12 13:50: run B evictions kicked in, freed 2 arenas (512MB each) but caused a 200ms P99 blip for ~10% of requests.
- 2025-06-18 09:10: run C tail-reserve prevented any raw-cudaMalloc fallbacks for a 24h steady-state.

Appendix: quick allocator pseudocode notes (informal):
- allocation request size S:
  1) try small-slab pool (fast-path): find free block in stream-affine slab list
  2) try same-arena-fit (reuse heuristics): prefer arenas with low hot-slot density
  3) if not found -> request CMA growth (atomic); on CMA grow failure -> raw cudaMalloc (record fallback)
  4) if fallback fails -> mark as retryable OOM and trigger async eviction job

Closing thoughts:
This series of sims shows that the observed production OOMs are not simple "not enough GPU memory" problems — they are emergent behavior from packing heuristics and the interaction of long-lived (KV) and short-lived (scratch) allocations under CMA. The short-term, low-risk mitigations (per-gpu tail reservation, per-stream small slabs, and fallback-based alerting) give substantial operational stability. Longer-term work (compaction, indirection, auto-tuning) will address the root cause but has higher implementation cost.

If reviewers want any of the raw run artifacts or visualization dashboards, point to linked_artifacts or ping me and I will share run tarballs and the slot-heatmap dashboards.

-- Priya
